question: Why doesn't every answer show products?
aliases: How does the shopper conversation work?
thesis: The agent answers first. Cards follow only when the catalog search finds a match: none, one, or a set that goes together.

fills.text: THE PROBLEM: Every reply opened with a canned "Got it! I recommend:" over a pile of product cards, so the chat read like an ad bot.

fills.alt: A shopper asks a question with one clear match and the agent answers with one product card and the reason for it
fills.caption: One clear match: one card, and a sentence saying why it fits.
fills.explain: A shopper asks something with one clear answer in the catalog. Watch the reply lead with the reason, then show a single card instead of a carousel. One intent gets one product, so the shopper isn't left comparing things they didn't ask for.

fills.alt: A question the catalog cannot resolve, answered in plain words with no product cards
fills.caption: Nothing in the catalog fits, so no cards: the agent just answers.
fills.explain: Here the question has no product answer. Watch for what doesn't appear: no cards, no forced recommendation, just a plain reply. The old panel put cards under every message; this one only shows products when retrieval actually found some.

fills.alt: Products that belong together arrive as a set in the chat
fills.caption: Products that only work together arrive as one set.
fills.explain: The shopper needs several items that belong together. Watch them arrive as a single set in the chat rather than as unrelated cards. The layout comes from what retrieval returned, not from a mode the shopper picked.

fills.text: HOW: Six months later I rebuilt the chat to read like a conversation: larger text, room between lines, and product names and prices in bold inside the reply. Cards appear only when the catalog search finds a match, as none, one, or a set. The three clips show each case.

fills.alt: The thinking state holds the shopper's place, then the reply fades in
fills.caption: While the agent works, the thinking state holds the shopper's place; then the reply fades in.
fills.explain: A static panel can't show that the agent is working. Watch the thinking state hold the spot where the answer will land, then the newest reply fade in word by word. The motion tells the shopper something is happening, and a static cue stays once it stops.

fills.alt: A product card confirms the add in place and shows the quantity from then on
fills.caption: Tap add and the card confirms in place, then keeps showing the quantity.
fills.explain: The shopper adds a product without leaving the conversation. Watch the card itself confirm the add and keep the quantity visible afterwards, so the tap visibly landed and the thread stays where it was.

question: Why did testing kill his favorite design?
aliases: How did user testing change the design?
thesis: Testing showed students skipped my tile grid and went looking for Instagram, so I cut it and fixed one problem per session until the bilingual version shipped.

fills.text: THE PROBLEM: I wanted enrollment to feel like an app: a student ID card that filled in as you chatted, and a bento grid of tiles so nobody had to think of a question first. It was a guess until students used it.

WHAT TESTING FOUND: Students skipped the tiles and kept asking "Do you have Instagram?" The tiles read as marketing; photos from real students did not. I cut the grid and the ID card, kept the form, the chat and the social links, then fixed one thing per session.
The first thing I do after talking to someone about a school is check out their Instagram. That tells me more than any brochure.

fills.explain: The top half runs at build time: sources, generators, the schema contract and the validator. The bottom half runs on every question: the answerer picks an answer, the layout engine cuts the stage, and the renderer morphs to it.

fills.text: CONTENT: Generators read the case-study data, public evidence records, commits and Figma exports. Every KPI is checked against its source text, and a validator gates shapes, assets, dashes, repeated numbers and backed problem statements.

THE STAGE: The answerer matches a starter question or merges the closest corpus units. The layout engine searches guillotine cuts snapped to a 12 x 12 grid, at most seven cells, sizing text with Pretext, and each new answer morphs from the strokes already on screen.

receipts.label: Guillotine cuts on a 12 x 12 grid, exact memoized search

fills.alt: Juniper stage design system: one ink color, type styles from the name to meta, spacing and grid limits, the stroke grammar and the morph timings
fills.caption: One color of ink, one weight of line.
fills.explain: Every value the renderer paints with is a Figma variable mirrored from the code, so if the two disagree text overflows. The stroke grammar and morph timings are drawn from the engine's own constants.
